{"id": "7:164/q14", "question": "What happened to the people who questioned further warnings?", "turns_on": "Whether their objection counts as resistance to sin or as culpable silence, and whether 7:165's silence about them establishes survival, doom or uncertainty.", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q14/p1", "position": "They survived along with the admonishers; only Sabbath offenders were punished.", "reasons": "Ikrima argues that questioners disliked and opposed the sin; reports say Ibn Abbas accepted this and gave him a cloak or two coarse garments. Al-Tha'labi argues the third-person 'they may fear' places the exchange among believers; al-Qurtubi cites 7:165 and 2:65, which name wrongdoers alone as punished. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and others accept their survival; Ibn Kathir prefers Ibn Abbas's later acceptance despite a good chain for the contrary report. Bursevi says certain despair would be needed to condemn the questioners. Al-Tabataba'i rejects Ikrima's inference: nonparticipation does not cancel the graver neglect of forbidding evil."}, {"id": "7:164/q14/p2", "position": "They perished with the offenders, although they had not themselves taken the fish.", "reasons": "One Ibn Abbas report says only warners escaped, linking the event to 2:66; another warns that silence at wrongdoing may merit the same fate. Al-Qurtubi records punishment for abandoning warning. Al-Tabataba'i argues that this omission was a graver sin and notes the silent group remained with the offenders while warners withdrew."}, {"id": "7:164/q14/p3", "position": "Their fate is not stated, so it remains unknown.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas repeatedly says 7:165 names the saved warners and punished wrongdoers but omits the third faction; he wept, feared for later silent witnesses, and wished to know their fate. Ikrima's counterargument subsequently moved him in other reports. Al-Qurtubi calls the unknown-fate reading apparent. Al-Tha'labi simply records disagreement."}, {"id": "7:164/q14/p4", "position": "The questioners were turned to stone.", "reasons": "Layth ibn Abi Sulaym transmits this distinct outcome."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q15", "question": "What happened after the warners withdrew from the Sabbath offenders?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q15/p1", "position": "The offenders became apes; their former neighbors recognized them, and some apes recognized and answered the warners.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd reports separation by a wall and David's curse; Ibn Abbas and Ikrima report shut doors the next morning, apes of all ages and sexes, weeping, nodding or recognizing named people before fleeing into the wilderness. Al-Baqir says the warners ultimately left town for fear of shared punishment. Ibn Ruman says the town was enclosed and the apes approached former neighbors. One Ibn Abbas report also mentions swine."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q16", "question": "What duty concerning wrongdoing does this verse teach?", "turns_on": "The scope of the duty when warnings appear unlikely to succeed, and the legal import of the fishing loophole.", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q16/p1", "position": "Believers must forbid wrong and continue sincere guidance even if success seems unlikely; their responsibility is the effort.", "reasons": "Al-Jubba'i qualifies the obligation as applying only while acceptance is not hopeless. Al-Tabataba'i says the warners had not fully despaired, so the duty remained, and charges the silent group with a graver failure. Elmalılı says abandoning a communal duty would implicate everyone and counsel may slow or soften wrong and its punishment. Kur'an Yolu makes the persistent admonishers the ideal, calls especially on learned believers to guide others, and says genuine educators must not assume vice incurable; prophets too answer for effort, while God grants guidance. Al-Umari says admonition remains an excuse even if rejected."}, {"id": "7:164/q16/p2", "position": "The episode supports the legal principle of blocking the means to a prohibited act.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi refers back to his discussion in al-Baqara."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q17", "question": "How does this dialogue connect with the surrounding verses and other passages?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection concerns the episode's immediate continuation or parallel language and legal themes elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q17/p1", "position": "It continues the Sabbath transgression account and shows persistent Israelite disobedience despite warnings.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i and al-Alusi connect it to 7:163; Elmalılı describes the righteous minority's circumstances; al-Tabataba'i situates the episodes in Israel's repeated covenant-breaking and later lax observance. Ibn Ashur says 7:165 supplies the outcome omitted in the compressed exchange. Study Quran sees the return to Israel's later disobedience and future punishment."}, {"id": "7:164/q17/p2", "position": "Its language or lessons are cross-referenced to other verses on excuse, admonition, rescue and forbidding wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi points to 9:66 for excuse; Ibn Ashur cites earlier uses of admonition at 4:63 and 7:145. Al-Qurtubi refers to 2:65 on transformation, 3:104 and 5:63 on forbidding wrong, and 4:140 on avoiding corrupt company. Asad compares the true admonishers with 7:159. Ibn Kathir notes he had presented village reports at al-Baqara."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q18", "question": "What other compositional features of the verse are noted?", "turns_on": "The notes address different compositional features.", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q18/p1", "position": "The response is a separate sentence because it is part of a dialogue.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains its separation on that syntactic and rhetorical basis."}, {"id": "7:164/q18/p2", "position": "The verse belongs to the Qur'an's extraordinary rhetorical composition.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani names novel composition and arrangement as his third proof of inimitability, to be detailed elsewhere."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q19", "question": "Where was this passage revealed?", "turns_on": "The extent assigned to the Madinan passage.", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q19/p1", "position": "It belongs to the three-verse exception to the otherwise Meccan sura, beginning at the town account.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi's Burhan extends that exceptional passage through the verse about the raised mountain."}, {"id": "7:164/q19/p2", "position": "Verses 163–167 were revealed in Madinah.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this judgment from Al and IJ."}]}
{"id": "7:164/q20", "question": "Which early transmitters reported the Sabbath village account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:164/q20/p1", "position": "Ibn Abbas's account is transmitted by al-Awfi, and Mujahid also transmitted the account.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says al-Awfi's transmission from Ibn Abbas resembles the preceding report; he also records Mujahid's transmission of the Ibn Abbas account."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q01", "question": "What does their forgetting of the reminder mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q01/p1", "position": "They deliberately abandoned or disregarded the warning, acting as though it had been forgotten.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies the ban on fishing; Ibn Jurayj connects the reminder to the believers in 7:164. Al-Zajjāj and al-Bayḍāwī allow comparison with literal forgetting. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls forgetting the strongest form of leaving; al-Qurṭubī compares 9:67. Abū Ḥayyān stresses the pronoun refers to the warned offenders. Al-Biqāʿī says they ignored the threatened consequence. Al-Ālūsī prefers a metaphor over a causal metonymy and excludes innocent literal lapse; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 6:44. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says repeated sin weakens the reminder until it ceases to affect them. Al-Itqān glosses dhikr as admonition."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q02", "question": "What does mā in 'what they were reminded of' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether mā names the reminded object or can stand for the reminding or its contents.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q02/p1", "position": "It is a relative pronoun referring to the thing they were reminded about.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn call this the apparent construction; al-Ālūsī agrees while allowing a verbal noun."}, {"id": "7:165/q02/p2", "position": "It may denote the act of reminding or admonition itself.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya offers the verbal-noun reading; Abū Ḥayyān and the Shaykh find it unpersuasive, while al-Ālūsī allows it."}, {"id": "7:165/q02/p3", "position": "It may denote the subject matter or contents of the reminder.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes this from the reminder itself; Abū Ḥayyān and the Shaykh say the analysis is not apparent."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q03", "question": "Which groups were saved or seized, and what became of the group that questioned further warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the questioners' objection counted as condemning evil, and whether the verse's silence about them implies rescue, punishment, or no conclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q03/p1", "position": "The warners and the group that questioned further warnings were saved; the fishers alone were punished.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says the questioners condemned the sin, and Ibn ʿAbbās accepted his inference and gave him cloaks. Al-Ḥasan says their mention of threatened punishment was itself warning, and killing a believer is graver than eating fish. Ibn Kathīr prefers Ibn ʿAbbās's later view despite a sound alternative report; the verse names only fishers as seized. Al-Rāzī invokes the communal nature of forbidding evil. Al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr count both groups as warners; some had stopped when warnings seemed futile. Al-Nasafī includes questioners among the saved."}, {"id": "7:165/q03/p2", "position": "Only the active forbidders were saved; both the offenders and the silent or questioning group perished.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls this the strongest warning against neglecting the duty. {"id": "7:165/q04", "question": "How many factions did the townspeople form?", "turns_on": "Whether the questioners in 7:164 are a separate group or belong with the warners.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q04/p1", "position": "Three: fishers, active admonishers, and abstainers who questioned or did not continue admonishing.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī prefers this because the admonishers say 'perhaps they will fear God' in the preceding verse, speaking of the sinners in the third person. Ibn Kathīr describes withdrawal of the warners. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a version with those who desisted and withdrew, those who stayed without sinning, and sinners."}, {"id": "7:165/q04/p2", "position": "Two: Sabbath offenders and believers who refrained and warned, including the concerned questioners.", "reasons": "The two-faction account treats the question to the warners as coming from within the righteous faction; al-Wāḥidī argues against this from its third-person phrasing."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q05", "question": "What is the evil that was forbidden?", "turns_on": "General lexical scope versus the particular Sabbath act in this story.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q05/p1", "position": "It is disobedience and sin, especially making what God forbade lawful.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls it sins; al-Ṭabarī mentions disobedience and legalizing the forbidden. Al-Māwardī says the reminder enjoined right and forbade wrong. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say this is the word's general scope."}, {"id": "7:165/q05/p2", "position": "In this incident it specifically means fishing for Sabbath fish.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān distinguish the story's particular offense from the general sense of evil; Bursevī says the forbidders forbade fishing."}, {"id": "7:165/q05/p3", "position": "The precise wrong forbidden is left unstated in one Ibn ʿAbbās query.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās asking what specific evil the admonishers had forbidden."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q06", "question": "Who are the 'wrongdoers,' and why are they called that?", "turns_on": "Whether omission of the silent group from the explicit seizure excludes it or its failure to intervene counts as wrongdoing.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q06/p1", "position": "They are the Sabbath fishers who disobeyed God and treated the ban as lawful.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies fishing and eating prohibited fish; al-Thaʿlabī and Abū Ḥayyān say the title points to the cause of seizure. Ibn ʿĀshūr says disobedience wrongs one's own soul by denying God's right to obedience."}, {"id": "7:165/q06/p2", "position": "They may include those who stayed silent and failed to forbid or leave wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the verse explicitly names only the fishers as seized, yet silent complicity may fall within 'wrongdoers'; he argues failure to admonish or shun makes one liable."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q07", "question": "What does baʾīs describe the punishment as?", "turns_on": "Which sense of the baʾs/buʾs root is foregrounded: severity, vileness, poverty, or destruction.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q07/p1", "position": "Severe, painful, grievous punishment.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Qatāda give severe and painful; Ibn ʿAbbās says aching or without mercy. Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and al-Thaʿlabī derive it from baʾs or buʾs, intensity. Al-Fārisī distinguishes a severe adjective from a verbal noun for distress; Abū Zayd distinguishes formidable baʾs from poverty forms. Al-Rāghib notes hardship and punitive calamity. Ibn Kathīr regards the painful and severe glosses as close; Ibn ʿĀshūr says all readings signify severe harm. Dhū al-Aṣbaʿ's verse witnesses the term."}, {"id": "7:165/q07/p2", "position": "Bad or vile punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash gives bad or vile; ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān cites banāt bīs for worthless things. The blame-verb readings yield 'bad is the punishment.'"}, {"id": "7:165/q07/p3", "position": "A punishment marked by poverty or misery.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this gloss. Abū Zayd and al-Rāghib distinguish poverty and hardship senses of buʾs and baʾsāʾ; Elmalılı understands a punishment that wrings them with poverty."}, {"id": "7:165/q07/p4", "position": "A destructive punishment.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this gloss to al-Akhfash."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q08", "question": "How is baʾīs read?", "turns_on": "Differences in hamza, vowel, yāʾ, and pattern; authorities test forms against attested Arabic morphology, poetic witnesses, and transmission chains.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q08/p1", "position": "Baʾīs, with open bāʾ, hamza kasra and following yāʾ, on faʿīl.", "reasons": "Ascribed to Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ and many others. Al-Ṭabarī prefers it because exegetes agree on severity; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim prefer its familiar adjectival shape. Dhū al-Aṣbaʿ's line supports it. It can be an intensive adjective or a verbal noun used adjectivally. Abū Bakr doubted his earlier attribution to ʿĀṣim and took this from al-Aʿmash; later routes preserve both."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p2", "position": "Biʾīs, the faʿīl form with kasra on bāʾ.", "reasons": "Attributed to some Meccans or Ibn Kathīr; grammarians explain first-radical kasra before a guttural second radical, and Abū Ḥātim calls it a dialect. Al-Samīn reports a Tamīm dialect."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p3", "position": "Bīs, with kasra on bāʾ, still yāʾ, no hamza, and nunation.", "reasons": "The Medinan, Nāfiʿ and Abū Jaʿfar form. Al-Kisāʾī derives it by easing hamza in baʾīs, bringing together and reducing two yāʾs; Muḥammad ibn Yazīd derives it from biʾs by moving its kasra. Al-Fārisī cites Sibawayh's heard usage and explains the unpronounceable quiescent hamza. Other analyses treat it as a transferred verb or softened hamza; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares dhīb from dhiʾb."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p4", "position": "Biʾs, with kasra on bāʾ, still hamza and nunation, on faʿl.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀmir articulates the hamza where Nāfiʿ has yāʾ. Some derive it by shortening baʾīs; others treat a past verb as a noun and adjective, or coin an adjective like ḥilf. Al-Fārisī compares qīl and qāl. Abū Ḥātim objects to a blame verb lacking its complement; al-Naḥḥās permits ellipsis ('a vile punishment'), while al-Samīn defends the normal requirement."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p5", "position": "Bayʾas or bayiʾs, with open bāʾ, still yāʾ and open hamza, on fayʿal or fīʿal.", "reasons": "Reported from Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash; Imruʾ al-Qays's line is cited. Abū Bakr later doubted the attribution. Al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī object that fayʿal generally has a weak middle radical; Ibn Jinnī invokes hamza's affinity to weak letters. Other witnesses compare ṣayqal, ḍaygham and ḥaydar. Qiraat ER calls it metathesis."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p6", "position": "Bayʾis, like the preceding fayʿil form but with kasra on hamza.", "reasons": "Attributed to some Kufans, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Aʿmash; al-Ṭabarī cites Imruʾ al-Qays for kasra yet calls the form anomalous for a sound root. Basran grammarians and Ibn ʿAṭiyya object to its pattern; al-Ālūsī also doubts its transmission. Rare counterexamples and hamza's affinity to weak letters are offered."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p7", "position": "Biʾs, with open bāʾ, kasra on hamza, and kasra nunation on sīn.", "reasons": "Reported from Basrans, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and others; Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt's verse attests hardship or affliction in this form."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p8", "position": "Biʾsa or bīsa, with kasra bāʾ and open final sīn, as a verb of blame.", "reasons": "Reported from al-Ḥasan and a variant from Nāfiʿ. It yields 'bad is the punishment.' Abū Ḥātim says it requires an overt subject or complement; al-Naḥḥās cites ellipsis such as fa-bihā wa-niʿmat to supply 'punishment.' Al-Samīn nevertheless favors the normal requirement."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p9", "position": "Biʾs with open bāʾ, kasra hamza and open sīn.", "reasons": "Yaʿqūb transmits it from some readers; comparable readings are attributed to ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Zayd ibn ʿAlī, with patterns shahid or kabid."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p10", "position": "Bāʾis, with long ā and hamza, on fāʿil.", "reasons": "Attributed to Mujāhid, Abū Rajāʾ and Abū al-Mutawakkil; al-Ālūsī says the form may mean one possessing strength."}, {"id": "7:165/q08/p11", "position": "Bīs or bays with open bāʾ and unhamzated yāʾ, either still or open.", "reasons": "Reported from Khārija from Nāfiʿ, Ubayy, Abū Iyās, Ṭalḥa and Naṣr routes. Some derive it by hamza easing and deletion, or by transferring hamza's vowel to yāʾ; the open yāʾ may remain because its vowel is incidental. Reports differ about final

{"id": "7:165/q09", "question": "What punishment was inflicted, and how does it relate to the transformation in 7:166?", "turns_on": "Whether 7:166 explains the torment named here or narrates a later, harsher stage.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q09/p1", "position": "The severe punishment was the transformation into apes, and in some reports swine; 7:166 explains it.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Dāmghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī identify the torment with metamorphosis. One Ibn ʿAbbās account says both apes and swine; Qatāda says young became apes and old swine. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 7:166 restates the offense while specifying the punishment. Abū ʿUbayda's gloss of khāsiʾīn is driven away or expelled."}, {"id": "7:165/q09/p2", "position": "A severe punishment came first; continued defiance brought the later transformation.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī explicitly puts torment before metamorphosis. Al-Rāzī calls them distinct. Al-Bayḍāwī says the surface sequence supports two stages; Bursevī suggests the first did not exterminate them, so they increased in error. Ibn ʿĀshūr says later witnesses persisted and then received the harsher transformation."}, {"id": "7:165/q09/p3", "position": "God's seizure destroyed or punished the persistent Sabbath offenders for their transgression.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī describes destruction for making forbidden fish lawful; al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn Kathīr connect the punishment with repeated rejection of counsel. Ibn ʿAbbās says disobedience brought divine abandonment; al-Zajjāj says persistence intensified the trial. Al-Biqāʿī says the promised warning was fulfilled."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q10", "question": "What does fisq mean, and what caused the seizure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q10/p1", "position": "Fisq is habitual disobedience, departure from obedience, and transgression; it caused their punishment.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses it as disobedience; al-Ṭabarī specifies leaving obedience for sin. Bursevī adds injustice and aggression; al-Biqāʿī emphasizes renewed acts. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the punishment requital, and al-Bayḍāwī attributes it to transgressing God's command. Al-Zajjāj describes a defiant person as unresponsive to admonition."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q11", "question": "How does the final causal phrase attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q11/p1", "position": "It modifies 'We seized'; the two causal or accompanying prepositions can coexist because their meanings differ.", "reasons": "Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say the earlier bi introduces the severe punishment, whereas bi-mā supplies the cause; al-Ālūsī adds that wrongdoing itself compounds the wrong."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q12", "question": "Why is 'punishment' indefinite and why does the passage expand the account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q12/p1", "position": "Indefiniteness magnifies the punishment and its horror.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly gives this rhetorical effect."}, {"id": "7:165/q12/p2", "position": "The expanded wording intensifies the account while presenting the reminder and prohibition as the same matter.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the differing phrases multiply the forms of punishment and compares Labīd's repeated simile, judging the Qur'anic phrasing more eloquent and beneficial."}]}
{"id": "7:165/q13", "question": "What duty to oppose wrongdoing does this verse teach?", "turns_on": "Whether abstaining and disapproving suffices once active warners have acted, or whether one must admonish or withdraw.", "positions": [{"id": "7:165/q13/p1", "position": "Forbidding wrong is a communal duty; performance by some discharges it for the others.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives the communal-obligation rule; the Turkish commentary extends forms of opposition to force, speech and writing.
